[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Primary Key Constraint in SQL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Primary Key constraint is a fundamental concept in relational database management systems (RDBMS) like SQL. It uniquely identifies each record in a table, ensuring data integrity and enabling efficient data retrieval. A table can have only one primary key."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Purpose of Primary Key"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Uniquely identifies each record in a table."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ensures that no two rows have the same primary key value."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Does not allow NULL values."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Enforces data integrity."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Used for establishing relationships between tables (foreign keys)."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Primary Key"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"A primary key can be defined when creating a table or added to an existing table. Let's explore both scenarios."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Defining Primary Key During Table Creation"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can define a primary key directly within the `CREATE TABLE` statement. Here's how:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE Employees (
    EmployeeID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName VARCHAR(255),
    LastName VARCHAR(255),
    Email VARCHAR(255)
);"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, `EmployeeID` is designated as the primary key.  Alternatively, you can define the primary key using a constraint:"},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE Employees (
    EmployeeID INT,
    FirstName VARCHAR(255),
    LastName VARCHAR(255),
    Email VARCHAR(255),
    CONSTRAINT PK_EmployeeID PRIMARY KEY (EmployeeID)
);"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, `PK_EmployeeID` is the name of the primary key constraint.  It's good practice to name your constraints for easier management and debugging."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Adding a Primary Key to an Existing Table"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"To add a primary key to an existing table, use the `ALTER TABLE` statement:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"ALTER TABLE Employees
ADD CONSTRAINT PK_EmployeeID PRIMARY KEY (EmployeeID);"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"This statement adds a primary key constraint named `PK_EmployeeID` to the `Employees` table, using the `EmployeeID` column."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Composite Primary Key"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"A composite primary key consists of two or more columns that, when combined, uniquely identify each record.  Individual columns in a composite key *can* contain duplicate values, but the combination of values across all columns must be unique."},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE OrderItems (
    OrderID INT,
    ProductID INT,
    Quantity INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, ProductID)
);"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, the combination of `OrderID` and `ProductID` uniquely identifies each item in an order. An order can contain multiple of the same product, but each `OrderID`, `ProductID` combination must be unique."},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"To add a composite primary key to an existing table:"},{"order":26,"type":"code","text":"ALTER TABLE OrderItems
ADD CONSTRAINT PK_OrderItems PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, ProductID);"},{"order":27,"type":"subheading","text":"Dropping a Primary Key"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"To remove a primary key constraint, use the `ALTER TABLE` statement with the `DROP CONSTRAINT` clause:"},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"ALTER TABLE Employees
DROP CONSTRAINT PK_EmployeeID;"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you didn't explicitly name the primary key constraint, some database systems might automatically assign a name. You'll need to determine the constraint name (often through system views or metadata queries) to drop it. For example, in MySQL, you might drop the primary key like this:"},{"order":31,"type":"code","text":"ALTER TABLE Employees
DROP PRIMARY KEY;"},{"order":32,"type":"subheading","text":"Important Considerations"},{"order":33,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Choose a column (or columns) that will always be unique and never contain NULL values for your primary key."},{"order":34,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Primary keys are often integer-based and auto-incrementing (e.g., using `AUTO_INCREMENT` in MySQL or `IDENTITY` in SQL Server) to simplify key generation."},{"order":35,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid using columns that are frequently updated as primary keys, as this can impact performance."},{"order":36,"type":"bullet_point","text":"When designing your database schema, carefully consider the relationships between tables and how primary keys will be used as foreign keys in other tables."},{"order":37,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":38,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Primary Key constraint is a cornerstone of relational database design. Understanding how to define, use, and manage primary keys is crucial for building robust and reliable database applications."}]
